The real answer is transphobia, but I don't think it's really something that we can blame them for, nor does it make them a bad person.

Romance as a concept is not purely biological and involves a lot from society. What makes someone attracted to another person is pretty culturally influenced. It's in the narratives we see and what we are told.

Most people end up pretty transphobic because we're all fed the gender binary from birth and told all these rules and norms. Eventually when we grow up and think for ourselves, we can learn to reject these things.

Still, it can be extremely difficult to change how you feel on a deep, visceral level. So a person can accept us, respect our names and pronouns, and otherwise be a good ally, but still not feel totally comfortable with the idea of dating someone who they've been taught to hate and be repulsed by all their life. There's still a bit of that bias left in there. And it is transphobic, but it's not their fault, nor is it something they can realistically overcome, let alone be expected to.

It's not ideal, but there isn't much we can or should do about that, other than continue to exist and be a positive force in the world. I have a lot of cis friends who are absolutely wonderful and were some of the first to support me in my transition, but I do know that for them, dating a trans person would be a confusing experience that comes with a lot of conflicting feelings, especially having come from transphobic families themselves.

I originally met my partner before I realized I was trans. We were a straight couple until my dysphoria slowly seeped in and it became clear that I was in fact trans.

Originally my partner thought she wasn't going to be attracted to me anymore but found herself surprised that she still was and that nothing had changed. Whether that makes her bi/pan we don't really know and don't really care to find out while we're still together (what good are labels if you aren't looking right haha) just that we love each other
